personality_voice.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore is warm, unhurried, and layered. He deploys humor as a social tool - the troll-hag-leprechaun joke, the chamber pot anecdote to Karkaroff, his mock-deafness when Harry calls Skeeter a 'cow', his remark about brother Aberforth and the goat. He is calm under acute pressure (calmly questioning Harry after the Goblet announces his name, calmly pressing Fudge while radiating dangerous power in the hospital wing). He is also capable of visible coldness and fury - the narration describing his face when he stuns fake-Moody as 'more terrible than Harry could have ever imagined', cold fury in every line. His speech patterns are measured, often gently ironic, and he uses rhetorical questions and digressions deliberately. He is capable of admitting uncertainty ('I have a theory, no more than that'), of voicing bitterness about the Longbottoms ('a bitterness Harry had never heard there before'), and of showing genuine emotional cost when he mentions the Diggorys. He strategises constantly - already in contact with Sirius, suggesting the cave, knowing about Harry's scar from Sirius, noting Harry's impulse to owl Sirius before Harry voices it.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the warmth, the wit (the curtain-burning anecdote in the dormitory scene is a good match), the capacity for firm authority ('Silence!'), and the calm-under-pressure register in several scenes (the post-maze interrogation of fake-Moody, the hospital wing confrontation with Fudge). The 'Priori Incantatem' explanation retains his measured, informative tone. However, the film introduces a significant vocal/behavioural departure in the Goblet scene: Dumbledore grabs Harry physically and shouts 'Harry! Did you put your name in the Goblet of Fire?!' in an urgent, almost aggressive register. This directly contradicts the book's explicit notation that he 'asked calmly'. The film also strips almost entirely the ironic, digressive humour that is a structural feature of his speech (the troll joke, the Aberforth-goat story, the Karkaroff chamber-pot riff, the mock-deafness moment). These are not isolated jokes - they are the primary evidence in the corpus of how his mind works and how he uses language to defuse, charm, and assert status.
personality_voice.difference: The aggressive Goblet interrogation is the most documented single deviation. The systematic removal of Dumbledore's ironic-digressive humour means the film retains the outer shell of authority and warmth but not the texture of his voice. The strategic subterranean intelligence (knowing about Sirius's cave, already mobilising before the crisis breaks) is absent from the film's dialogue, making him appear more reactive.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The Goblet interrogation is directly evidenced as a contradiction of a named book trait ('asked calmly' vs. shouted and grabbed). The loss of the humour pattern is evidenced by its complete absence across many film scenes where book equivalents exist. These changes are not cosmetic - the calm under pressure and the ironic wit are the two most distinctive features of his voice in the corpus. The film Dumbledore is recognisable but a simplified and occasionally tonally opposite version. Score lands at 17: recognisable but with important tonal/trait losses.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore's narrative role in GoF is multi-layered. He is the institutional authority who enables the tournament, but also the covert strategist operating several moves ahead of everyone else: he has been corresponding with Sirius, suggested the cave, is already reading the signs (getting Moody out of retirement), and by the end of the year is immediately pivoting to rebuild the Order - recruiting Sirius, dispatching Snape, commissioning Hagrid and Maxime for a mission, pressing Fudge with a specific five-point action plan. He initiates action constantly: he leads Harry to the forest when Crouch appears, he is the one who blasts open the door to Moody's office, he immediately takes charge of the Barty Crouch Jr. interrogation, he runs the post-revelation hospital wing sequence. He also serves as the moral-intellectual explainer: the Pensieve sequence is entirely his construction, he explains Priori Incantatem, he explains the connection between Harry and Voldemort, he explains the Neville situation. He is the structural fulcrum around which the entire revelation plot resolves.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves his role as institutional authority, his presence at key moments (the Goblet selection, the first task, the second task, the graveyard return, the Moody reveal, the Fudge confrontation), and the interrogation of Barty Jr. He retains agency in the Moody office - physically blasting the door, demanding answers. The Fudge confrontation is compressed but preserves his willingness to confront power. However, the entire strategic layer is removed: no sign of Sirius correspondence, no hint he has been reading the signs before the crisis, no commissioning of Hagrid/Maxime, no dispatching of Snape to a task. The Pensieve's function is radically changed (see below). The Order-building sequence is absent.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The film removes Dumbledore's proactive strategic agency entirely. The book version is already in motion - the film version reacts. The Sirius coordination, the Snape mission, the Hagrid/Maxime mission, the Order mobilisation speech, and the full action-plan delivered to Fudge (remove dementors, send envoys to giants, recall Sirius's allies) are all absent. His role as explainer is also compressed - the Pensieve explanation of Priori Incantatem is reduced to a single line.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: These are not peripheral scenes. Dumbledore's proactive mobilisation in the final chapters is one of his primary narrative functions in GoF - it establishes him as the counter-force to Voldemort. Its absence means the film Dumbledore is reactive where the book Dumbledore is directive. Some agency is retained (the Moody reveal, the Fudge confrontation) so this is not a total loss, but it is substantial. Score: 13.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in GoF are: protecting Harry (inviting Moody, monitoring via Sirius, telling Harry to go to Gryffindor Tower and not owl), preparing for Voldemort's return (reading the signs, mobilising before others believe it), institutional responsibility (running the tournament fairly, defending Hogwarts' reputation), and a deep commitment to truth over comfort (refusing to soften Cedric's death at the feast, pressing Fudge even when it ends their alliance). There is internal tension: he uses Harry as a de facto intelligence asset (asking him to recount the graveyard immediately, over Sirius's objection) while also expressing genuine protectiveness and guilt ('I put you in terrible danger this year, Harry'). The Pensieve scene shows another layer - he is himself overwhelmed by too many threads and uncertainties, extracting thoughts to analyse them. He is not omniscient; he is working hard to stay ahead.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the commitment-to-truth motivation (the feast speech, pressing Fudge), the protective impulse (the dormitory scene, the hospital wing), and the guilt ('I put you in terrible danger'). The preparedness-for-Voldemort motivation is partially visible but not explained. The internal tension around using Harry while protecting him survives in vestigial form.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film loses the 'working to stay ahead' dimension - the Pensieve in the film is used to show Harry the Barty Jr. trial (a plot device), not as evidence of Dumbledore's own cognitive overload and uncertainty. The book's 'I have a theory, no more than that' humility and the active processing of too much information are absent. His motivation to mobilise others (the Order-building) disappears with that plot material.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations survive. The simplification is real but does not reverse or replace what is there. Score: 11.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in GoF is intentionally largely flat - he begins the year as a strategically aware, quietly concerned figure and ends it as a galvanised leader prepared to split with Fudge and rebuild the resistance. The arc is less about internal change and more about the transition from hidden concern to open action. The key turning point is the moment he sees fake-Moody drag Harry away and immediately knows something is wrong - his cold fury in the office is the culmination of a year of suppressed dread becoming open emergency response. His final speeches (feast, hospital wing) represent a new phase: he is now publicly committed to a course that will cost him his relationship with the Ministry.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film tracks this arc adequately if thinly. He is concerned throughout, takes charge at the crisis, confronts Fudge, delivers the truth-telling feast speech, and ends with a quieter personal moment with Harry ('Dark and difficult times lie ahead... you have friends here'). The arc from watchful concern to open confrontation is present.
character_arc.difference: The transition is compressed. The book's arc from 'worried more than I've seen him' (Hagrid's observation) through the terrifying moment of fury in Moody's office to the full mobilisation sequence is telescoped. The film skips the mobilisation endpoint, so the arc stops at confrontation-with-Fudge rather than active resistance-building.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The core arc is present and its key beats are hit, though compressed and without the culminating mobilisation. Score: 13 - compressed but recognisably faithful.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The three primary relationships evidenced in the corpus are: (1) Harry - characterised by protectiveness, trust, genuine warmth, but also a willingness to demand things of Harry that cost him (requiring the graveyard account immediately, overriding Sirius). (2) Fudge - collegial surface over deep disagreement; Dumbledore is patient until he isn't, then explicitly confrontational and willing to break. (3) Snape - trust that goes unexplained, a visible apprehension as Snape departs on his mission, a dynamic of deliberate opacity toward others. Secondary: Sirius (active secret collaboration), Hagrid (long loyalty, protectiveness), Karkaroff (polite surface, mutual wariness). The Harry relationship is most important and shows both warmth and a calculated demand for adult engagement ('understanding is the first step to acceptance').
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Fudge confrontation is well preserved. The Harry relationship retains warmth and the key post-graveyard scene, including the guilt admission. The Snape relationship is present (dispatching him, watching with apprehension). However, the Sirius relationship is entirely absent - the secret correspondence, the cave suggestion, the shared strategy are gone. The Hagrid relationship is reduced to plot function. The Harry relationship loses the specific texture of demanding Harry recount the trauma immediately over Sirius's explicit objection - a key beat that shows the tension between Dumbledore's protectiveness and his strategic necessity.
key_relationships.difference: The Sirius collaboration relationship is entirely removed from the film. The Harry relationship loses its most complex moment (the insistence on the immediate account). These are not marginal - the Sirius collaboration is a significant part of how Dumbledore's proactive intelligence is evidenced, and the Harry-trauma-account scene is the best single demonstration of the tension within his protectiveness.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly present but with meaningful simplification and one complete omission (Sirius). Score: 7.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The corpus shows several layers of Dumbledore's complexity beyond the 'wise headmaster' surface: (1) Strategic opacity - he knows far more than he reveals to Harry (Sirius, the cave, the signs), creating a gap between his calm exterior and his active concern. (2) Ironic self-awareness - the chamber pot anecdote shows he knows his own eccentricity and uses it; the Aberforth story is self-deprecating while making a serious point. (3) Moral weight in small decisions - his choice to give Hagrid and Snape second chances is not incidental but thematic. (4) The Pensieve as cognitive tool - he is not omniscient but effortful. (5) The glimpsed 'gleam of triumph' when Harry describes Voldemort using his blood - a moment of moral complexity, a hidden calculation that the reader sees but Harry almost misses. (6) His bitterness about the Longbottoms is a crack in his usual composure. (7) The farewell to Snape with 'a trace of apprehension on his face' - showing genuine vulnerability about whether his trust is justified.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains the ironic warmth (curtain anecdote), the moral authority (feast speech), and the post-revelation gravity. The 'gleam of triumph' moment is absent - the film's equivalent scene has no such beat. The Pensieve is reframed as a trial-replay device rather than a cognitive overflow tool, removing the complexity of Dumbledore being overwhelmed. The strategic depth (Sirius, Snape's mission apprehension) is absent. The Hagrid/second-chances theme is not developed.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film removes: the gleam of triumph (morally complex micro-moment), the Pensieve-as-cognitive-overload characterisation, the strategic opacity shown through the Sirius correspondence, the visible apprehension about Snape, the bitterness about the Longbottoms, and most of the ironic-digressive humour. What remains is a Dumbledore who is wise, warm, and principled - accurate as far as it goes, but stripped of the contradictions and hidden calculations that make the book version genuinely complex.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The absent material is not decorative - it constitutes the primary evidence for Dumbledore's complexity in this book. The gleam of triumph alone is one of the most important characterisation moments in the entire series. The film gives a faithful surface and loses almost all of what is beneath it. Score: 8.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75) considered: a core act of agency - the post-revelation Order mobilisation, the dispatch of Snape, and the five-point Fudge action plan - is not transferred to another character but simply removed. This represents Dumbledore's primary narrative function in the book's final act. Cap 3 threshold is met and the final score of 69 falls below 75.
Cap 1 (score above 85) considered and inapplicable given score range.
key_observations: The film's Dumbledore is recognisably faithful in broad strokes - the warmth, the moral authority, the willingness to confront Fudge, the post-crisis care for Harry are all present. The two most damaging deviations are: (1) the Goblet scene, where the film replaces the book's explicitly noted calm with physical aggression and shouting, directly contradicting a named trait; and (2) the systematic removal of the proactive strategic layer that defines Dumbledore's role in the second half of the book. The film gives us a Dumbledore who reacts wisely to crises; the book gives us one who has been quietly preparing for and managing them all year. The 'gleam of triumph' is the single most significant lost nuance - it is the one moment in the corpus that complicates Dumbledore's relationship with Harry beyond simple benevolence. Its absence, combined with the removal of the ironic-digressive humour pattern and the Pensieve's reframing from cognitive tool to plot device, produces a Dumbledore who is simplified into a noble authority figure rather than a layered, strategically calculating, self-aware, and occasionally morally ambiguous one.
